Author: topstockalerts
Text: Jim Cramer said Wall Street may be overreacting to the threat posed by Meta’s Muse AI agent to consumer companies, creating potential opportunities among stocks that have been broadly sold off. The so-called “consumer inertia” trade assumes AI agents could hurt businesses that benefit when customers fail to cancel subscriptions, compare prices or shop around for better deals. Since Muse launched Sept. 8, Planet Fitness has fallen 20%, while Airbnb and Booking Holdings are down 13% and 16%, respectively. SiriusXM has dropped about 11%, Charles Schwab 9% and Life Time 7%. Cramer argued that investors should assess each company’s actual exposure to AI rather than treating entire industries as potential losers. He pointed to Life Time as an example, saying its highly engaged members may be less likely to cancel than Planet Fitness customers. In travel, Cramer said online agencies retain value through features such as rewards programs and easy price comparisons. $META

Text: AI executives clashed with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei during a White House meeting, exposing divisions over AI safety and regulation. According to The Wall Street Journal, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang challenged Amodei over his warnings about AI risks, while Amodei defended greater transparency regarding cyber threats and potential labor-market disruption. The dispute reflects broader opposition to industry rules that could slow growth or concentrate regulatory power. Author: topstockalerts
Text: Wells Fargo analyst Ken Gawrelski raised his price target on Meta Platforms to $1,000 from $796, making it the highest target among analysts tracked by FactSet. The upgrade reflects expectations that Meta’s artificial-intelligence investments, including its Muse AI assistant, can drive substantial earnings growth despite near-term pressure on profits. Gawrelski expects Meta’s third-quarter EPS to fall to $3.72, partly due to an anticipated $10 billion legal-settlement charge. The company is also facing higher AI infrastructure spending, which could weigh on profitability in the near term. However, Wells Fargo believes these costs are positioning Meta for much stronger growth through 2028. The firm sees the combination of AI monetization, improving infrastructure efficiency and continued growth across Meta’s advertising ecosystem as potential catalysts for a major expansion in earnings and valuation. $META

Text: $APLD Very bullish earnings call. Wes expects more than 600 MW online over the next 12 months and another 250 MW of expansion leases signed by year end. On those leases, he’s looking for rent increases ABOVE 15%, possibly with longer terms. This is mega. APLD delivered 250 MW over the past year. Now they expect to deliver more than twice that over the next year. Polaris Forge 1 (Ellendale, ND - AI factory leased to $CRWV) already has 250 MW operating of the 400 MW contracted there. A few other things stood out for me 1. About $36 billion in contracted revenue across five AI factory campuses in 3 states. Approximately $86B if all renewal options are exercised. Polaris Forge 3 (Center, ND AI factory leased to $META) , and Delta Forge 1 and 2 (Boyce, LA and Brookwood, AL AI factory leased to $META) all have the same tier-one investment-grade hyperscaler. We know that hyperscaler is $META from public records although Wes did not confirm it. 2. Construction of all 400 MW at Polaris Forge 1 and the contracted 200 MW at Polaris Forge 2 (Harwood, ND AI factory leased to $ORCL) is fully funded. The latest $1.59B PF1 financing was at 7% interest, compared with 9.25% on the earlier PF1 debt. I like seeing the borrowing costs come down as they prove they can deliver these buildings. 3. They’re working on financing PF3, DF1 and DF2 through Macquarie preferred equity and project debt, with APLD keeping majority ownership. Management sounded confident about the terms it can get with that investment-grade tenant ($META) behind the leases. Those financings still need to close. 4. Base HPC rental income in Q1 was $65.8M, up about 49% in ONE quarter. HPC net operating income was $58.8M, with an 89% margin. And most of the 1.4 GW contracted capacity still has to come online. Adjusted EBITDA was $64.4M, excluding $CHRN. Total revenue was $341.9M, up 322%, including $183.5M of tenant fit-out work. 5. APLD finished the quarter with about $2.95B in cash plus $728M in restricted cash, against roughly $6.4B of debt. More than 80% of debt principal doesn’t mature until fiscal 2031 or later. 6. Wes sees a path to roughly 2 GW operating by the end of 2028 AND 3.5 to 4 GW by the end of 2030 - the second half was NEW news. DF1 is targeting initial operations in the first half of 2027. There is a lot of construction ahead, but we’re starting to see what this company should look like in a few years. 7. APLD signed a power agreement for a planned 1,200 MW gas plant to support PF3 expansion, with deliveries expected from 2030. APLD also owns about 10% of Base Electron. That could give them a lot more room to expandl in North Dakota. 8. Finland gives $APLD access to up to 1 GW of potential power, with initial availability expected in 2028. Limited upfront exposure, and they’re already talking to hyperscalers about the site. They looked at 30-40 sites before choosing this one. 9. Wes said he expects ALL of the big 4 hyperscalers will eventually lease AI factories from $APLD in North Dakota. 10. The more community opposition there is to the datacenters of APLD’s competitors the MORE valuable APLD (with its massive permitted AI factories and low community opposition) becomes. 11. Don’t overlook $CHRN. APLD owns approximately 96%. It has a planned 50 MW Microsoft deployment, and Wes says it’s on track for $1B in annual recurring revenue in 2027. He also sees potential for several hundred MW during 2027 to 28, separate from APLD’s large campuses. 12. To secure the pipeline, $APLD reserved roughly FOUR years of entire factory output from some suppliers. Wes also said the facilities are designed for 30-yyplus years of use and to accommodate changing equipment. 13. The rent increases were probably the most encouraging part of the call for me. If APLD can sign the next leases at the pricing Wes is seeking, while continuing to bring down their financing costs, I think there is a lot more upside here. The big theme of the call was APLD is executing well to turn all of that contracted revenue into real revenue. I still see this as a LONG term investment with the big payoff in 2028 when everything under contract is built and generating revenue. Not financial advice. Everyone must do their own due diligence. Author: 10xorbust
Text: $APLD Yes, I’ve read what’s public as part of my DD. Only the $CRWV leases have been publicly disclosed and filed with the SEC although of course they are in redacted form. The contents of the other leases have been disclosed in $APLD filings in terms of the characterizations of them. And yes, tenants CAN terminate the leases IF $APLD misses the delivery deadlines in the contracts. $CRWV and $ORCL both have that protection. There are grace periods, possible extensions and notice requirements, so missing a target date doesn’t automatically give the tenant a way out. For $CRWV’s first two leases, $APLD specifically says a qualifying delivery failure can let the tenant terminate the lease without a termination fee or further lease payments. For the remaining 150 MW building, there is a July 29, 2027 deadline for the first three halls to meet the required commencement conditions. Some of the details are redacted, so I wouldn’t pretend we can see every exception. For $ORCL, there is a cancellation right if delivery runs more than 150 days late against phased dates starting October 1, 2026. Fitch also reports an $ORCL parent guarantee and rights to terminate for chronic outages. But $ORCL’s actual agreements are not public, so I don’t know every notice requirement or exactly what $ORCL would owe when using one of those exits. For the $META projects at Delta Forge 1, Delta Forge 2 and Polaris Forge 3, I’ve read the public disclosures. I haven’t seen the actual tenant leases which are NOT available. To be clear, $APLD has never acknowledged $META as the tenant but Wells Fargo reported it, and I have reported it too from mine and other’s examinations of the publicly available filings. ￼ We know $APLD acknowledges construction-delay cancellation risk, but we don’t have those projects’ specific deadlines, exceptions or guarantee terms. I’m not going to claim I’ve reviewed clauses that haven’t been released. If a tenant simply changes its plans, that’s expensive. APLD says voluntary cancellation by the tenant requires payment of the entire remaining contract value. $CRWV’s clause is explicit: 100% of the remaining scheduled base rent, plus specified taxes, paid before the cancellation takes effect. That payment requirement is separate from its rights to terminate the lease for delivery failures, uncured $APLD defaults, major property damage or condemnation. The lease values are roughly $11B for $CRWV , $5B for $ORCL and $20.2B across the $META projects, over 15 years. Most have three optional five-year renewals; $ORCL has two. I count the roughly $36B of initial-term commitments separately from the much larger $85 billion figure that assumes every renewal gets exercised. There are also protections in the later $CRWV arrangements. Some leases moved to a subsidiary, with parent guarantees that kick in under specified circumstances. At ELN-02, if the subsidiary’s lease ends, the suspended parent lease resumes for those halls. Moving the lease into a subsidiary doesn’t, by itself, make the parent’s commitment disappear. As we all know, the KEY factor to $APLD raking in this huge pile of revenue is on time construction execution. So far, $APLD has executed its construction milestones flawlessly. There’s no guarantee $APLD will continue to do that but I’m quite optimistic given it’s spotless to date track record. $APLD already has the first 250 MW for $CRWV operating at Polaris Forge 1 and has projected completing another 600 MW within the next 12 months. These lease contracts make it expensive for tenants to change their minds, but $APLD still must finish the remaining buildings on time and keep them running as promised. I take the backlog seriously. The delivery deadlines are part of the deal too.

The S&P 500 gained an average of 15.1% in the 12 months after midterm elections. That was almost twice the average gain over similar periods in other years. These are two different ways of measuring returns, but both show that stocks have tended to do well after midterms. https://www.capitalgroup.com/advisor/insights/articles/midterm-elections-markets-5-charts.html The gains have often started before the election year ends. A study in The Journal of Wealth Management found especially strong returns in the last three months of the midterm year and the first six months of the next year. Author: KavaStocks
Text: $APLD $CRWV $META Meta reports Wednesday, and Applied Digital and CoreWeave both have a lot riding on it. The APLD board has speculated that Meta is the customer behind the company's three newest campuses and offered some great evidence for it. The filings check out. The tenant on the Delta Forge 2 county paperwork is registered at 1 Meta Way. Applied has already said all three campuses share one customer, so more than half of its contract book would sit with Meta. It's still unofficial, which is how hyperscalers tend to like it. Meta matters on the CoreWeave side, too. It's one of CoreWeave's biggest customers, and a Meta contract backed the first investment-grade loan CoreWeave ever landed. Applied's credit work on the Ellendale leases came right behind that loan. On that side of the book, CoreWeave is the middleman. This week the market went after the middleman, and the backdrop gave it plenty of reason. The Fed went back to hiking in September, Wednesday's inflation print ran hot, and the odds of a second hike at the October 28 meeting went from about one in five to roughly a coin flip. Money rotated out of AI and chips, which is how the Dow finished the week up while the Nasdaq pulled back a week after it set a record. Oracle, the Korean memory names, and the neoclouds all sold off on worries about how the buildout gets financed and what that money costs. CoreWeave's unsecured 2031s traded as low as 78 cents on the dollar, yielding more than 16 percent, while the 10-year fell almost a quarter of a point. Rising hike odds and a falling 10-year read to me like a market pricing a Fed that tightens into a slowdown, which is a bad combination for the biggest borrower in the group. Applied's exposure runs through Ellendale. CoreWeave is the weakest credit on a tenant list where everyone else is investment grade, and its bear case was always going to live in the interest line. Last quarter that interest bill ran about five times its adjusted operating income. CoreWeave will be back in the market for money for at least the next couple of years, and the cheapest door it has left depends on rating agencies feeling generous in a tape like this. I'm not waving that off. Then I pulled up the landlord paper, which was a lot calmer. The 7 percent notes from June, the ones funding the third Ellendale building, slipped about a point to 94.5. CoreWeave is the tenant behind those notes and the borrower behind its own 2031s, yet at the lows their yields were about eight percentage points apart. Most of that gap is collateral. The Ellendale noteholders have a lien on the building and its lease, and CoreWeave needs that capacity to serve its own customers. CoreWeave's unsecured holders get paid after everyone with collateral. Cipher's secured notes, with no CoreWeave behind them, barely moved off par. That tells me the people who get paid first are pricing this as a CoreWeave problem. The stocks didn't sort any of it out. Landlords with no CoreWeave exposure got sold right alongside Applied and Galaxy, and I'd have been surprised by anything else. The landlords themselves stand about where their bonds do. If I got to pick how a credit scare in this sector plays out, I'd pick something close to this week, with the most levered name's unsecured debt taking the hit while the paper secured by buildings mostly holds. The risk I'm left with sits in the stretch where interest is already on the books and the rent is still catching up. A building slipping now gives a tenant under pressure an opening to revisit the lease, and the financing for the next campuses gets priced in this tape. If the landlord notes start following CoreWeave's unsecured debt down, the structure isn't providing the protection I'm counting on, and the bond quotes would show it well before a lease does. Meta goes first on Wednesday. If the spending holds, the money keeps moving down the line. A capex cut or softer talk about renting outside capacity would hit everyone below it, and Applied twice. The Fed meets a week later, CoreWeave reports a couple of weeks after that, and I'll read its interest line before I look at the backlog. It's an uncomfortable spot to be in. The parts of the structure I can check held up this week, and I own the equity, which is last in line behind all of it. The stock and the structure can stay out of sync for a while, and this kind of selloff will probably return every time CoreWeave raises money. I can live with that as long as the landlord notes stay where they are.

Author: CycleTrade
Text: $META da day is past and we are in the post. But let's examine 200 sma entries/exits vs VWAP entries in tiny time frames However, on a 1-minute intraday chart, the short-term consensus leans heavily toward VWAP (Volume Weighted Average Price) as the more important tactical compass for immediate execution. Why VWAP rules the 1-minute chart: Intraday momentum traders treat VWAP as the ultimate benchmark for fair value during the session. Being above or below VWAP dictates immediate institutional bias, intraday trend health, and short-term mean reversion. If price is holding cleanly above VWAP on a 1-minute time frame, intraday longs are favored because volume backs the upward push. Where the 200-period SMA fits: On a 1-minute chart, a 200-period simple moving average acts more like a macro trend filter or structural support/resistance line rather than an immediate trading trigger. While staying above a higher-timeframe or longer-period SMA keeps you on the right side of the broader trend, it is often too lagging for precise micro-entries compared to VWAP and fast volatility bands. The verdict: Use VWAP to manage intraday entries, risk, and immediate momentum bias, while keeping an eye on the 200 SMA simply to confirm whether the larger intraday trend supports the position.
